newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Some British votes are more equal than others.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Some British votes are more equal than others.

text.p: If you live in Bishop's Road in Hayes, you belong to a small group of voters which could make a difference to the outcome of Britain's May 1 election.
For despite a national voters' roll of 44 million, Britain's electoral system bestows enormous influence on just a few thousand people in strategic areas of the country.

It's odds-on that some of these crucial voters live in this quiet residential street of semi-detached brick homes with neat gardens in west London, a quiet corner close to the hubbub of Heathrow airport.
While each vote in Hayes and Harlington constituency carries great weight, first-past-the-post voting effectively disenfranchises huge swathes of the British public.
A few miles (km) towards central London, in the stately streets of Kensington and Chelsea, support for the ruling Conservative party is so solid that a vote for anybody else counts for nothing.

Under the Westminster system, Britain is carved into 659 geographical constituencies and the candidate with most votes in each area wins a parliamentary seat. Ballots for other candidates in the constituency are disregarded.
This vests enormous importance in constituencies where the parties are neck-and-neck, the "key marginals" such as Hayes and Harlington where the election will be effectively decided.

If at the 1992 election just 27 people had voted Labour instead of Conservative, then Labour would have won. As it was, Conservative candidate Terry Dicks prevailed with a majority of 53 and took the seat for the next five years.

"We fight for every vote that might be out there, " said Sue Hull, Labour's campaign manager in the constituency. "We are not going to lose it this time," she told Reuters at Labour's mission control in a converted shop in the town centre.
ENERGY CONCENTRATED IN MARGINAL SEATS
Across Britain, the big parties know where they can count on rock-solid support and where they must fight for a result. In this way, votes carry widely differing degrees of importance.
One estimate put the number of voters who affected the 1992 election, when the Conservatives won a 21-seat majority, at just 40,000.

The big publicity effort focuses on the marginals, while the safe seats are left to their own devices. Voters in marginals are peppered with phone calls and pamphlets from every party. Cabinet ministers come to call almost every day.

Most opinion polls, which show the percentage of the population supporting each party, have Labour far ahead. But they are uncertain indicators of support. Labour requires a 4.3 percent swing nationwide to win but the swing is never uniform. A party can win a seat with 66 percent of the vote in one part of the country and just 34 percent in another.
In 1983, when Margaret Thatcher's Conservatives won 188 more seats than Labour, the ruling party attracted the votes of just 13.01 million voters from a total electorate of 30.7 million.

A major party need not contest seats it knows it has no chance of winning as taking a few percent of the vote counts for nothing. This leads to tactical voting by electors which distorts the picture of party support nationwide.
The Westminster system has few supporters other than the main beneficiaries, the big two parties.

"You would find it difficult to find anybody in the academic establishment who would support the current system...According to some calculations, the outcome of the last election was decided by as few as 1,200 people," said political scientist David Denver, of the University of Lancaster.
"There are now very few countries left in the world which use this system. Emerging democracies are much more likely to adopt a system of proportional representation," he told Reuters.
ANOMALIES
Many other anomalies creep into the current British system.

According to the calculations of political scientists Michael Thrasher and Colin Rallings at the University of Plymouth, Labour would emerge almost 40 seats ahead of the Conservatives if they won equal shares of the national vote.
The Conservatives would be unlikely to achieve an absolute majority in parliament on less than 42 percent of the vote, while Labour could win with a 38 percent share.
In the February 1974 election, Labour won less votes than the Conservatives but ended up as the biggest party in parliament.

The big parties have gained a disproportionate level of parliamentary representation at the expense of smaller parties such as the Liberal Democrats, who always gain a far lower percentage of seats in parliament than is reflected in their national share of the popular vote.

Not surprisingly, the Liberal Democrats are long-standing supporters of a change to proportional representation, supported by political and constitutional reform groups such as the Electoral Reform Society and Charter 88.
Denver said a Labour victory in the election would increase the likelihood of electoral reform within the next decade.
"They are committed to some kind of change...I would be very disappointed if they did not follow it through," he said.
